rubric.why: Identifies electronic configuration as the arrangement of electrons.
rubric.description: States that electronic configuration is the arrangement of an atom’s electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the arrangement of electrons.

rubric.why: Specifies where the electrons are arranged.
rubric.description: Mentions that electrons are arranged in different shells or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying shells or energy levels.

modelAnswer: Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in the different shells of an atom.

items.followUp: What is meant by nuclear charge?

rubric.why: Identifies the inner-shell electrons responsible for shielding.
rubric.description: States that inner-shell electrons are involved in the shielding effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning inner-shell electrons.

rubric.why: Explains how shielding affects the attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons.
rubric.description: Explains that inner electrons reduce the nuclear attraction felt by outer electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the reduced attraction or shielding of outer electrons.

modelAnswer: The shielding effect is the reduction in the nuclear attraction experienced by outer-shell electrons due to repulsion by inner-shell electrons.

rubric.why: Includes the energy change associated with electron gain.
rubric.description: States that energy is released when the atom gains an electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the release of energy.

rubric.why: Specifies the atom’s state when it accepts the electron.
rubric.description: States that a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying the gaseous atom accepting an electron.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.

rubric.why: Identifies the basis Moseley introduced in place of atomic mass.
rubric.description: States that atomic number replaced atomic mass as the basis for arranging elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming atomic number as the new basis.

rubric.why: States the revised relationship between properties and atomic number.
rubric.description: States that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the revised periodic relationship.

modelAnswer: Moseley showed that elements should be arranged according to increasing atomic number instead of atomic mass.
The periodic law was amended to state that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

items.followUp: Why do metals conduct heat well?

rubric.why: Identifies the charge carriers in metals.
rubric.description: Mentions that metals contain free or mobile electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the free electrons.

rubric.why: Explains how the electrons enable electrical conduction.
rubric.description: Explains that these electrons move through the metal and carry electric charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking electron movement to conduction.

modelAnswer: Metals contain free electrons that can move through the metal lattice.
These mobile electrons carry electric charge, so metals conduct electricity.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a polar covalent bond and a non-polar covalent bond.

rubric.why: Defines a lone pair as a pair not shared in bonding.
rubric.description: States that a lone pair is a pair of valence electrons not shared with another atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the unshared electron pair.

rubric.why: Defines a bond pair as electrons shared between atoms.
rubric.description: States that a bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the shared electron pair.

modelAnswer: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that is not shared with another atom.
A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.

items.followUp: What type of covalent bond is formed in an oxygen molecule?

rubric.why: Identifies the bond type in the nitrogen molecule.
rubric.description: States that a triple covalent bond is formed in a nitrogen molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the triple bond.

rubric.why: Explains the triple bond in terms of shared electrons.
rubric.description: States that the two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that three electron pairs are shared.

modelAnswer: A nitrogen molecule has a triple covalent bond between its two nitrogen atoms.
The atoms share three pairs of electrons.

items.followUp: Define allotropy and give an example of an allotrope of oxygen.

rubric.why: States that an element can occur in multiple forms.
rubric.description: Defines allotropy as the existence of an element in two or more forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an element exists in multiple forms.

rubric.why: Includes the condition or a valid example of allotropy.
rubric.description: States that the forms occur in the same physical state, or gives a valid example such as diamond and graphite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the same-state condition or a correct example.

modelAnswer: Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
For example, carbon exists as diamond and graphite.
